title: Bridging the Gap: LEO Satellite Internet and Human Rights
gist: LEO satellite internet has become de facto critical infrastructure for besieged states and civil society, but CSIS argues its concentration in a handful of U.S.-based operators creates a single-shutoff risk demonstrated by Starlink complying with Uganda's shutdown order while defying Iran's, and Russia's Kalinka jamming weapon shows counterspace countermeasures are already degrading the technology in the field.

insights.claim: LEO satellites orbit at 1,200 miles or less versus more than 22,000 miles for GEO, which cuts launch cost, limits interference, and delivers materially faster connectivity.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The orbital-altitude gap is the structural reason legacy GEO satellite operators face permanent competitive impairment in broadband.
insights.quote: LEO satellites orbit at 1,200 miles or less above sea level, limiting interference, making them less expensive to launch, and allowing for faster connectivity.
insights.locator: Q1: What is LEO satellite internet

insights.claim: Amazon Leo has been tested at up to 1 gigabit per second while common GEO systems reach maximum speeds of only 10 to 15 percent of that.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A near order-of-magnitude throughput advantage means GEO capacity is being stranded, with implications for incumbent satellite operators' asset values.
insights.quote: While Amazon’s LEO system (called Amazon Leo) has been tested at up to 1 gigabit per second, common GEO systems reach maximum speeds of 10–15 percent of that.

insights.claim: LEO constellations neutralize infrastructure gaps by making the network's location dynamic and hard to target, which is why they are displacing terrestrial infrastructure in conflict and remote-coverage use cases.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defines the demand driver: LEO is bought for survivability, not just speed, which supports premium pricing in conflict and frontier markets.
insights.quote: In short, LEO satellites remove the potential for infrastructure gaps by making their location dynamic and difficult to target, and they can operate largely free of government interference.
insights.locator: The predictability and speed of LEO satellite internet

insights.claim: Starlink went live in Ukraine roughly 12 hours after a public Twitter request from Ukraine's minister of digital transformation, showing private operators can deliver national-scale connectivity on timescales no state procurement can match.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Establishes speed-to-deploy as the private sector's structural advantage in crisis connectivity, and the reason governments accept dependency risk.
insights.quote: Approximately 12 hours later, Musk confirmed that the world’s most prominent low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite internet was now active in the country.
insights.locator: Just a few days into Russia's full-scale invasion

insights.claim: SpaceX approached the Pentagon for financing only several months after providing Starlink in Ukraine, once Ukrainian forces had already become reliant on the technology, illustrating a dependency-then-repricing pattern.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A repeatable commercial playbook: establish operational dependency in a crisis, then convert it into government contract revenue.
insights.quote: Several months after initially providing Starlink access in Ukraine, SpaceX reached out to the Pentagon requesting financing. This took place after the Ukrainian resistance had already become reliant on the technology.
insights.locator: The speed with which Musk's SpaceX was able

insights.claim: Musk personally intervened more than a year into Russia's full-scale invasion to limit Starlink access for the Ukrainian military ahead of a specific Crimea operation, demonstrating that individual discretion can override military planning.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Key-man risk in critical infrastructure is a real and demonstrated operational variable, not a governance abstraction.
insights.quote: Musk intervened personally to limit Starlink access to the Ukrainian military in advance of a particular operation in Crimea.
insights.locator: Beyond funding is the potentially capricious nature

insights.claim: Starlink complied with Uganda's January 2026 order to cease operations ahead of an election-period internet shutdown while simultaneously continuing to serve Iranian protesters despite the service being legally prohibited in Iran, showing operator responses to authoritarian orders are inconsistent and discretionary.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Compliance behavior is unpredictable case by case, which makes regulatory and reputational exposure for satellite operators difficult to underwrite.
insights.quote: Starlink chose to comply with one authoritarian government attempting to shut down the internet while ignoring the orders of another, leaving civil society without internet in one setting but keeping those in the other connected.
insights.locator: In short, Starlink chose to comply

insights.claim: Private-sector-led critical infrastructure gives companies significant influence over vital aspects of governance and foreign policy, in the same way electricity or water utilities would if privately controlled.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Sets up the regulatory thesis: satellite internet operators are drifting toward utility-style oversight, with the margin and autonomy costs that implies.
insights.quote: When an actor beholden to incentives and constituencies outside of the public good controls critical infrastructure, gaps are created.
insights.locator: Critical infrastructure is, by its very definition, critical

insights.claim: A Russian-developed weapon called Kalinka is the most likely cause of degraded Starlink performance during the 2026 Iran protests, creating a zone effect that both limits LEO satellite functionality and complicates replacing satellites in orbit.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Proliferating LEO jamming weapons cap the reliability premium buyers will pay for satellite connectivity in contested theaters.
insights.quote: a Russian-developed weapon known as Kalinka, which creates a “zone effect” that both limits the functionality of LEO satellites and makes it difficult to replace them in orbit
insights.locator: The "most likely culprit" of this limitation

insights.claim: Russia and China have both invested heavily in counterspace capabilities, with Beijing developing lasers to burn or blind satellite sensors and Moscow fielding additional signal jammers beyond Kalinka.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Counterspace is a two-power investment program, implying sustained demand for satellite hardening and resilient-comms defense spending.
insights.quote: Beijing has worked to develop lasers that can burn or blind satellite censors, causing malfunctions.
insights.locator: Kalinka is not the only technology

insights.claim: Any counter-LEO technology that proves effective at silencing dissent is highly likely to diffuse to other authoritarian actors, given the recent history of authoritarian collaboration.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Expect the addressable set of jamming-exposed markets to widen fast, which is the core downside risk to LEO revenue growth in the developing world.
insights.quote: Both the Iran protests and recent history of authoritarian collaboration create a high likelihood that any technologies that are effective in silencing dissent and facilitating repression will be available for use by other authoritarian actors.
insights.locator: Both the Iran protests and recent history

insights.claim: Ukraine's military has few realistic alternatives to LEO satellite internet because Russia has systematically destroyed Ukrainian terrestrial infrastructure, making the overreliance risk concrete rather than theoretical.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Locked-in demand supports revenue durability for the incumbent operator but concentrates strategic risk for the customer.
insights.quote: Given Russia’s approach to destroying Ukrainian infrastructure, there are precious few other options for Ukraine’s military beyond LEO satellite internet.
insights.locator: This approach to the technology of strategic competition

insights.claim: The two largest LEO satellite internet companies are based in the United States with smaller players in the EU and Canada, giving Western governments direct legal leverage over the entire commercially relevant industry.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional concentration means one legislative move in Washington can reset operating rules for global satellite connectivity.
insights.quote: The two largest LEO satellite internet companies are based in the United States, with smaller companies based in the EU and Canada.
insights.locator: The World Liberty Congress, a collection of human rights defenders

insights.claim: Satellite operators' reliance on federal procurement dollars for continued operations gives Washington strong leverage to impose weapons-industry-style conduct requirements on them.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Federal contract dependence is the lever regulators will pull first, so conduct conditions are likelier to arrive via procurement terms than new statute.
insights.quote: Their reliance on federal procurement dollars for continued operations creates added incentive for compliance.
insights.locator: Just as weapons companies are subject to limitations

insights.claim: The proposed policy direction is to treat internet access as a public good and human right enforceable through international courts, following UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres's call for universal internet access by 2030 as a basic human right.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A rights-based framework would create legal liability for shutdowns and pressure operators to resist host-government orders, changing their compliance calculus.
insights.quote: universal access to the Internet by 2030 as a basic human right
insights.locator: To start, this effort requires an inclusive

insights.claim: Human rights organizations are pushing to engineer out single-switch shutoffs entirely, with the World Liberty Congress's Tech for Freedom initiative producing a manifesto against centralization and a decentralized social media site.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Decentralization pressure is a structural headwind to platform and constellation operators whose value rests on centralized control points.
insights.locator: Third, in line with a rights-based approach
